orig_9709_p3_cx_cartesian.description: Separate the two components, calculate in Cartesian form and use the conjugate to turn a complex denominator into a real one.

sections.title: What do the two components represent?
sections.label: Cartesian form
sections.intro: The definition \(\mathrm i^2=-1\) extends the real numbers. Every complex number has a unique Cartesian form.

blocks.html: Two complex numbers are equal when their real parts agree and their imaginary parts agree. On an Argand diagram \(a+b\mathrm i\) goes at \((a,b)\).

figure.alt: The points z at (3,2) and z star at (3,-2) on an Argand diagram, reflected in the real axis.
figure.caption: Conjugation keeps the horizontal position and changes the vertical sign.

blocks.html: \(\operatorname{Im}(a+b\mathrm i)=b\). The coefficient is \(b\); leave out the imaginary unit.

blocks.title: Read the two components
blocks.prompt: For \(z=7 - 2 \mathrm{i}\), give \(\operatorname{Re}z\) and \(\operatorname{Im}z\).
blocks.hint: Read the signed coefficient of i, without the i.
blocks.solution:
The Cartesian form is \(a+b\mathrm i\). The real part is the term without \(\mathrm i\).

The imaginary part is the real coefficient of \(\mathrm i\), so the two values are \(7\) and \(-2\).

sections.title: Which components move under addition and subtraction?
sections.label: Addition and subtraction
sections.intro: Adding a fixed complex number translates every point by the same two components. Subtracting translates by the opposite displacement.

blocks.html: \((a+b\mathrm i)+(c+d\mathrm i)=(a+c)+(b+d)\mathrm i\). Subtract the two pairs component by component.
When subtracting a complex number, change both terms in the second bracket.

blocks.title: Add or subtract matching components
blocks.prompt: Calculate \((6 - 4 \mathrm{i})-(-2 - 3 \mathrm{i})\). Give the pair (real part, imaginary part).
blocks.hint: Keep the brackets when subtracting.
blocks.solution:
Combine the real parts: \(6-(-2)=8\).

Do the same for the imaginary parts: \(-4-(-3)=-1\).

The result is \(8 - \mathrm{i}\).

sections.title: Where does the imaginary product go after expanding?
sections.label: Cartesian products
sections.intro: Expand using the same distributive rule used for real algebra. The one new step is to simplify the product of the two imaginary terms.

blocks.html: \((a+b\mathrm i)(c+d\mathrm i)=(ac-bd)+(ad+bc)\mathrm i\). Work from the expansion when showing how you got the answer.
The product of two imaginary terms contributes \(-bd\) to the real part.

blocks.title: Expand a Cartesian product
blocks.prompt: Multiply \(\left(5 + 2 \mathrm{i}\right)\left(2 - 3 \mathrm{i}\right)\). Give the pair (real part, imaginary part).

retry.feedback: Replace i squared by minus one. This changes the sign of the product of the two imaginary terms.

blocks.hint: The term involving i squared belongs to the real part.
blocks.solution:
Use all four terms. The product of the two imaginary terms is \(6\) because \(\mathrm i^2=-1\).

The real part is \((5)(2)-(2)(-3)=16\).

The cross terms give imaginary part \((5)(-3)+(2)(2)=-11\), so the product is \(16 - 11 \mathrm{i}\).

blocks.html: Show the expansion so that the four terms and the sign of the real product are visible.

sections.title: Why is a number times its conjugate real?
sections.label: Conjugates on Argand
sections.intro: Reflect the point in the real axis. Its two imaginary components now cancel in a sum and its product has no imaginary cross term.

blocks.html: \(z^*=a-b\mathrm i\) and \(zz^*=a^2+b^2\). The product is strictly positive whenever \(z\ne0\).
The negative of \(z\) changes both components. Its conjugate changes one.

blocks.title: Reflect in the real axis
blocks.prompt: For \(z=4 - 7 \mathrm{i}\), give \(z^*\) as (real part, imaginary part), then calculate \(zz^*\).
blocks.hint: Conjugation reverses only the imaginary part.
blocks.solution:
Keep the real component and change the sign of the imaginary component. This gives \(z^*=4 + 7 \mathrm{i}\).

The cross terms cancel in the product, leaving \((a+b\mathrm i)(a-b\mathrm i)=a^2+b^2\).

Here the product is \(65\).

sections.title: How can I divide by a complex number?
sections.label: Rationalise with the conjugate
sections.intro: Divide by a real denominator after multiplying by a suitable form of one.

blocks.html: Use \(\frac{c-d\mathrm i}{c-d\mathrm i}=1\) when \(c+d\mathrm i\ne0\). The new denominator is \(c^2+d^2\).
Multiply the numerator as a whole. The operation applies to both real and imaginary terms.

blocks.title: Make the denominator real
blocks.prompt: Express \(\frac{7 + \mathrm{i}}{3 - 2 \mathrm{i}}\) as a (real part, imaginary part) pair.

retry.feedback: This is the reciprocal quotient. Keep the numerator above the original denominator.

blocks.hint: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the original denominator.
blocks.solution:
Multiply numerator and denominator by \(3 + 2 \mathrm{i}\). This keeps the ratio unchanged.

The denominator becomes \(13\) and the numerator becomes \(19 + 17 \mathrm{i}\).

Divide both components by \(13\) to obtain \(\frac{19}{13} + \frac{17 \mathrm{i}}{13}\).

blocks.html: Check your result by multiplying it back by the original denominator.

sections.title: How can equality recover two unknown coefficients?
sections.label: Recover a hidden number
sections.intro: Convert every term to Cartesian form, then compare the two real equations.

blocks.html: For real \(a,b,u,v\) and \(z=u+v\mathrm i\), the expression \(az+bz^*\) is \((a+b)u+(a-b)v\mathrm i\).
The sign in the second coefficient is a difference because the conjugate reverses the imaginary term.

blocks.title: Recover a complex number from its conjugate
blocks.prompt: Let \(z=u+v\mathrm i\), with real \(u,v\). If \(5z+2z^*=14 + 9 \mathrm{i}\), find \(z\) as a (real part, imaginary part) pair.
blocks.hint: Conjugating changes the sign of v i. Equate the two real equations separately.
blocks.solution:
The left side is \((a+b)u+(a-b)v\mathrm i\) for weights \(a=5,b=2\).

Equate the real terms and imaginary coefficients: \(7u=14\) and \(3v=9\).

Therefore \(z=2 + 3 \mathrm{i}\).

examples.title: Read the two components
examples.question: For \(z=-4 + 3 \mathrm{i}\), give \(\operatorname{Re}z\) and \(\operatorname{Im}z\).
solution: The Cartesian form is \(a+b\mathrm i\). The real part is the term without \(\mathrm i\).
The imaginary part is the real coefficient of \(\mathrm i\), so the two values are \(-4\) and \(3\).

examples.title: Add or subtract matching components
examples.question: Calculate \((2 + 5 \mathrm{i})+(-3 + 2 \mathrm{i})\). Give the pair (real part, imaginary part).
solution: Combine the real parts: \(2+(-3)=-1\).
Do the same for the imaginary parts: \(5+(2)=7\).
The result is \(-1 + 7 \mathrm{i}\).

examples.title: Add or subtract matching components
examples.question: Calculate \((4 - 3 \mathrm{i})-(2 + 4 \mathrm{i})\). Give the pair (real part, imaginary part).
solution: Combine the real parts: \(4-(2)=2\).
Do the same for the imaginary parts: \(-3-(4)=-7\).
The result is \(2 - 7 \mathrm{i}\).

examples.title: Expand a Cartesian product
examples.question: Multiply \(\left(3 - 2 \mathrm{i}\right)\left(-1 + 4 \mathrm{i}\right)\). Give the pair (real part, imaginary part).
solution: Use all four terms. The product of the two imaginary terms is \(8\) because \(\mathrm i^2=-1\).
The cross terms give imaginary part \((3)(4)+(-2)(-1)=14\), so the product is \(5 + 14 \mathrm{i}\).

examples.title: Reflect in the real axis
examples.question: For \(z=-2 + 6 \mathrm{i}\), give \(z^*\) as (real part, imaginary part), then calculate \(zz^*\).
solution: Keep the real component and change the sign of the imaginary component. This gives \(z^*=-2 - 6 \mathrm{i}\).
The cross terms cancel in the product, leaving \((a+b\mathrm i)(a-b\mathrm i)=a^2+b^2\).
Here the product is \(40\).

examples.title: Make the denominator real
examples.question: Express \(\frac{5 - 3 \mathrm{i}}{2 + \mathrm{i}}\) as a (real part, imaginary part) pair.
solution: Multiply numerator and denominator by \(2 - \mathrm{i}\). This keeps the ratio unchanged.
The denominator becomes \(5\) and the numerator becomes \(7 - 11 \mathrm{i}\).
Divide both components by \(5\) to obtain \(\frac{7}{5} - \frac{11 \mathrm{i}}{5}\).

examples.title: Recover a complex number from its conjugate
examples.question: Let \(z=u+v\mathrm i\), with real \(u,v\). If \(4z+1z^*=15 - 6 \mathrm{i}\), find \(z\) as a (real part, imaginary part) pair.
solution: The left side is \((a+b)u+(a-b)v\mathrm i\) for weights \(a=4,b=1\).
Equate the real terms and imaginary coefficients: \(5u=15\) and \(3v=-6\).
Therefore \(z=3 - 2 \mathrm{i}\).

glossary.definition: \(\mathrm i^2=-1\). It lets us solve equations with no real square root.
\(a+b\mathrm i\) with two real numbers \(a,b\).
The horizontal axis records the real component. The vertical axis records the imaginary component.
The reflection of \(a+b\mathrm i\) in the real axis is \(a-b\mathrm i\).

orig_9709_p3_cx_roots.description: Solve quadratics with negative discriminants, use conjugate pairs in real polynomials and find both exact Cartesian square roots.

sections.title: What changes when a discriminant is negative?
sections.label: Non-real solutions
sections.intro: The quadratic formula still gives two roots when the discriminant is negative. Replace a square root of a negative number by the imaginary unit times a positive real square root.

blocks.html: If \(d>0\), then the solutions of \(w^2=-d\) are \(w=\pm\mathrm i\sqrt d\).
The quadratic formula needs both signs. The negative discriminant does not make the equation unsolvable over the complex numbers.

blocks.title: Solve a quadratic with no real roots
blocks.prompt: Solve \(z^{2} - 8 z + 17=0\). Enter both pairs (real part, imaginary part).

fields.label: All root pairs (real part, imaginary part)

retry.feedback: You found one root. The other root has the same real part and the opposite imaginary part.

blocks.hint: After completing the square or using the formula, take both square roots of the negative number.
blocks.solution:
The discriminant is \(-4\). A negative discriminant gives two non-real roots.

The equivalent completed form is \((z-(4))^2=-1\). Its two square roots are \(\pm 1\mathrm i\).

Adding \(4\) gives \(4 + \mathrm{i},\quad 4 - \mathrm{i}\).

sections.title: When must another root be the conjugate?
sections.label: The real-coefficient condition
sections.intro: Conjugation respects each sum and product. With real coefficients, conjugating a polynomial value is the same as conjugating its input.

blocks.html: If \(p(z)=0\) and the coefficients of \(p\) are real, then \(p(z^*)=p(z)^*=0\). For a non-real root the two roots are distinct.
If the polynomial has a non-real coefficient, this reasoning does not apply. A real root is already its own conjugate.

blocks.title: Make a real quadratic factor
blocks.prompt: A real polynomial has root \(-3 + 2 \mathrm{i}\). Give its conjugate as the (real part, imaginary part) pair. Then enter a real quadratic equation with those two roots.
blocks.hint: Multiply the two factors as a difference of squares.
blocks.solution:
A real polynomial satisfies \(p(z^*)=p(z)^*\), so the conjugate \(-3 - 2 \mathrm{i}\) is also a root.

The corresponding factor is \((z-(-3))^2+4\), from the product of the conjugate factors.

On expansion this is \(z^{2} + 6 z + 13\).

sections.title: How does a conjugate pair reduce a cubic?
sections.label: Reduce a cubic
sections.intro: Replace two non-real linear factors by their real quadratic product. Division leaves a real linear factor when the original polynomial is cubic.

blocks.html: For roots \(a+b\mathrm i\) and \(a-b\mathrm i\), their monic factor is \((z-a)^2+b^2\).
The constant of the quadratic is the sum of the squares of the real and imaginary components.

blocks.title: Remove the known conjugate pair
blocks.prompt: The polynomial \(p(z)=z^{3} - 2 z^{2} - 3 z - 20\) has root \(-1 + 2 \mathrm{i}\). Give its conjugate as (real part, imaginary part), then give the remaining real root.

fields.label: Other non-real root (real part, imaginary part)

blocks.hint: Find the real quadratic factor from the conjugate pair before dividing.
blocks.solution:
The given root and its conjugate give the real factor \(z^{2} + 2 z + 5\).

Divide the polynomial by that factor. This gives \(z - 4\) with remainder zero.

The real root is \(4\).

sections.title: Which roots remain after removing the pair?
sections.label: Reduce a quartic
sections.intro: A quartic can leave either two real roots or a second conjugate pair after the known pair is removed. Solve the remaining quadratic to decide.

blocks.html: The known factor accounts for two degrees. Use the remaining degree to check that the final root list is complete.
Do not stop after stating the conjugate when the question asks for all roots.

blocks.title: Remove the known conjugate pair
blocks.prompt: The polynomial \(p(z)=z^{4} - 7 z^{3} + 15 z^{2} + z - 130\) has root \(2 + 3 \mathrm{i}\). Give its conjugate as (real part, imaginary part), then give the remaining real roots.

fields.label: Other non-real root (real part, imaginary part)

blocks.hint: Find the real quadratic factor from the conjugate pair before dividing.
blocks.solution:
The given root and its conjugate give the real factor \(z^{2} - 4 z + 13\).

Divide the polynomial by that factor. This gives \(z^{2} - 3 z - 10\) with remainder zero.

The real roots are \(-2,\quad 5\).

sections.title: How can I find both square roots in Cartesian form?
sections.label: Square the components
sections.intro: Set \(w=u+v\mathrm i\) and suppose \(w^2=A+B\mathrm i\). The comparison gives a difference of squares and a product.

blocks.html: \(u^2-v^2=A,\quad 2uv=B,\quad u^2+v^2=\sqrt{A^2+B^2}\). Add and subtract to get the two squared magnitudes. Then use the product to couple the signs.
The signs are linked. Giving one sign choice for each component independently would generally produce two extra values.

blocks.title: Pair the signs in two square roots
blocks.prompt: Find both square roots of \(-21 - 20 \mathrm{i}\). Enter each as (real part, imaginary part).

fields.label: All root pairs (real part, imaginary part)

retry.feedback: One root is correct. Its negative is a second root because the square is the same.

blocks.hint: Compute the sum and the difference of u squared and v squared, then check the sign of 2uv.
blocks.solution:
Set \(w=u+v\mathrm i\) with \(u,v\) real. Equating components gives \(u^2-v^2=-21\) and \(2uv=-20\).

Since \((u^2+v^2)^2=(u^2-v^2)^2+(2uv)^2\), we have \(u^2+v^2=29\).

Add and subtract the two squared-component equations to obtain \(u^2=4\) and \(v^2=25\).

Use the sign of the imaginary coefficient to pair the signs. The two roots are \(2 - 5 \mathrm{i},\quad -2 + 5 \mathrm{i}\).

blocks.html: Verify by squaring both proposed roots or by noting that the second root is the negative of the first.

sections.title: What happens when one component is zero?
sections.label: Square roots on an axis
sections.intro: For real input the imaginary coefficient of the square is zero, so at least one component of a root is zero.

blocks.html: If \(z>0\) is real its roots are real. If \(z<0\) is real its roots are purely imaginary. For zero the only distinct root is zero.
Avoid dividing by a component before checking whether it can vanish.

blocks.title: Pair the signs in two square roots
blocks.prompt: Find both square roots of \(36\). Enter each as (real part, imaginary part).

fields.label: All root pairs (real part, imaginary part)

retry.feedback: One root is correct. Its negative is a second root because the square is the same.

blocks.hint: Compute the sum and the difference of u squared and v squared, then check the sign of 2uv.
blocks.solution:
Set \(w=u+v\mathrm i\) with \(u,v\) real. Equating components gives \(u^2-v^2=36\) and \(2uv=0\).

Since \((u^2+v^2)^2=(u^2-v^2)^2+(2uv)^2\), we have \(u^2+v^2=36\).

Add and subtract the two squared-component equations to obtain \(u^2=36\) and \(v^2=0\).

Check the non-zero component directly. The two roots are \(6,\quad -6\).

examples.title: Solve a quadratic with no real roots
examples.question: Solve \(z^{2} - 6 z + 13=0\). Enter both pairs (real part, imaginary part).
solution: The discriminant is \(-16\). A negative discriminant gives two non-real roots.
The equivalent completed form is \((z-(3))^2=-4\). Its two square roots are \(\pm 2\mathrm i\).
Adding \(3\) gives \(3 + 2 \mathrm{i},\quad 3 - 2 \mathrm{i}\).

examples.title: Solve a quadratic with no real roots

solution: The discriminant is \(-144\). A negative discriminant gives two non-real roots.
The equivalent completed form is \((z-(-2))^2=-9\). Its two square roots are \(\pm 3\mathrm i\).
Adding \(-2\) gives \(-2 + 3 \mathrm{i},\quad -2 - 3 \mathrm{i}\).

examples.title: Make a real quadratic factor
examples.question: A real polynomial has root \(1 + 4 \mathrm{i}\). Give its conjugate as the (real part, imaginary part) pair. Then enter a real quadratic equation with those two roots.
solution: A real polynomial satisfies \(p(z^*)=p(z)^*\), so the conjugate \(1 - 4 \mathrm{i}\) is also a root.
The corresponding factor is \((z-(1))^2+16\), from the product of the conjugate factors.
On expansion this is \(z^{2} - 2 z + 17\).

examples.title: Remove the known conjugate pair
examples.question: The polynomial \(p(z)=z^{3} - z^{2} - 7 z + 15\) has root \(2 + \mathrm{i}\). Give its conjugate as (real part, imaginary part), then give the remaining real root.
solution: The given root and its conjugate give the real factor \(z^{2} - 4 z + 5\).
Divide the polynomial by that factor. This gives \(z + 3\) with remainder zero.
The real root is \(-3\).

examples.title: Remove the known conjugate pair
examples.question: The polynomial \(p(z)=z^{4} + 3 z^{3} + 7 z^{2} - 21 z - 26\) has root \(-2 + 3 \mathrm{i}\). Give its conjugate as (real part, imaginary part), then give the remaining real roots.
solution: The given root and its conjugate give the real factor \(z^{2} + 4 z + 13\).
Divide the polynomial by that factor. This gives \(z^{2} - z - 2\) with remainder zero.
The real roots are \(-1,\quad 2\).

examples.title: Pair the signs in two square roots
examples.question: Find both square roots of \(7 + 24 \mathrm{i}\). Enter each as (real part, imaginary part).
solution: Set \(w=u+v\mathrm i\) with \(u,v\) real. Equating components gives \(u^2-v^2=7\) and \(2uv=24\).
Add and subtract the two squared-component equations to obtain \(u^2=16\) and \(v^2=9\).
Use the sign of the imaginary coefficient to pair the signs. The two roots are \(4 + 3 \mathrm{i},\quad -4 - 3 \mathrm{i}\).

examples.title: Pair the signs in two square roots
examples.question: Find both square roots of \(-49\). Enter each as (real part, imaginary part).
solution: Set \(w=u+v\mathrm i\) with \(u,v\) real. Equating components gives \(u^2-v^2=-49\) and \(2uv=0\).
Add and subtract the two squared-component equations to obtain \(u^2=0\) and \(v^2=49\).
Check the non-zero component directly. The two roots are \(7 \mathrm{i},\quad - 7 \mathrm{i}\).

Set \(w=u+v\mathrm i\) with \(u,v\) real. Equating components gives \(u^2-v^2=-64\) and \(2uv=0\).

Since \((u^2+v^2)^2=(u^2-v^2)^2+(2uv)^2\), we have \(u^2+v^2=64\).

Add and subtract the two squared-component equations to obtain \(u^2=0\) and \(v^2=64\).

Check the non-zero component directly. The two roots are \(8 \mathrm{i},\quad - 8 \mathrm{i}\).

orig_9709_p3_cx_modulus_argument.description: Find exact distances and directions, choose the correct quadrant and move between Cartesian and modulus–argument descriptions.

sections.title: How do the two components give a distance?
sections.label: Modulus as distance
sections.intro: Plot the point on the Argand plane. Its two components are the signed horizontal and vertical displacements from the origin.

blocks.html: \(|a+b\mathrm i|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\) and \(|z|^2=zz^*\). The modulus of zero is zero.
The sum of the absolute values of the two components is generally a different distance.

blocks.title: Find distance from the origin
blocks.prompt: Find the modulus of \(5 - 12 \mathrm{i}\).

retry.feedback: That is the squared modulus. Take the non-negative square root.

blocks.hint: Use the non-negative square root of the sum of squares.
blocks.solution:
The two Cartesian components are \(5\) and \(-12\).

By Pythagoras the modulus is \(\sqrt{(5)^2+(-12)^2}=13\).

sections.title: How can I select the correct quadrant?
sections.label: Argument from coordinates
sections.intro: A positive turn from the positive real axis is anticlockwise. Start by marking the signs of the coordinates, then find an acute reference angle if the point is off the axes.

blocks.html: For non-zero real component, the reference angle has tangent \(\left|\frac ba\right|\). The quadrant determines how to convert that angle.

figure.alt: The ray through a point in quadrant II has an obtuse argument from the positive real axis and an acute reference angle from the negative real axis.
figure.caption: Locate the correct quadrant before choosing the argument.

blocks.html: The calculator can return an acute or negative angle with the same tangent but on the wrong ray.

blocks.title: Choose the argument in the stated interval
blocks.prompt: Find the exact argument of \(2 - 2 \sqrt{3} \mathrm{i}\) in radians with \(-\pi<\theta\le\pi\).

retry.feedback: This direction points along the opposite ray. Use the signs of both coordinates.

blocks.hint: Sketch the signs of the Cartesian components before using an acute reference angle.
blocks.solution:
Use the point \(\left(2,- 2 \sqrt{3}\right)\) to fix the direction.

The signs put the point in quadrant IV. The acute reference angle is \(\frac{\pi}{3}\). In the stated interval that gives \(- \frac{\pi}{3}\).

blocks.html: When an exact angle is required, connect the ratio of the components to a known trigonometric value.

sections.title: Which representative should I give?
sections.label: Intervals and axes
sections.intro: Adding a whole turn of \(2\pi\) leaves the direction unchanged. At the origin the direction is undefined.

blocks.html: Use the interval specified. The common choices are \(-\pi<\theta\le\pi\) and \(0\le\theta<2\pi\). On the negative real axis the argument is \(\pi\) in both.

RayArgument in the usual principal interval
Positive real\(0\)
Positive imaginary\(\frac{\pi}{2}\)
Negative real\(\pi\)
Negative imaginary\(-\frac{\pi}{2}\)
With \(-\pi<\theta\le\pi\), the included endpoint is \(\pi\).

blocks.title: Choose the argument in the stated interval
blocks.prompt: Find the exact argument of \(- 8 \mathrm{i}\) in radians with \(0\le\theta<2\pi\).

retry.feedback: This direction points along the opposite ray. Use the signs of both coordinates.

blocks.hint: Sketch the signs of the Cartesian components before using an acute reference angle.
blocks.solution:
Use the point \(\left(0,-8\right)\) to fix the direction.

The point lies on an axis. From the positive real axis, the required direction in the stated interval is \(\frac{3 \pi}{2}\).

sections.title: How can I recover signed coordinates?
sections.label: Back to Cartesian form
sections.intro: Take the projection of the radius onto each axis. The trigonometric signs already account for the quadrant.

blocks.html: For modulus \(r\) and angle \(\theta\), the point is \((r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\).
Keep the radius positive. A negative horizontal or vertical coordinate comes from the trigonometric function.

blocks.title: Recover Cartesian components from distance and direction
blocks.prompt: A point has modulus \(8\) and argument \(\frac{3 \pi}{4}\) radians. Give the (real part, imaginary part) pair.
blocks.hint: Cosine gives the horizontal component. Sine gives the vertical one.
blocks.solution:
The horizontal component is \(r\cos\theta\); the vertical component is \(r\sin\theta\).

The two components are \(- 4 \sqrt{2}\) and \(4 \sqrt{2}\). Thus the number is \(- 4 \sqrt{2} + 4 \sqrt{2} \mathrm{i}\).

sections.title: What is the difference between position and displacement?
sections.label: Distance between two points
sections.intro: For points corresponding to \(a\) and \(b\), start at \(a\) and move by \(b-a\) to reach \(b\).

blocks.html: The distance is \(|b-a|\); the direction of the movement, when the points differ, is \(\arg(b-a)\).
Reversing the subtraction leaves distance fixed but changes the direction.

blocks.title: Use the Argand displacement between two points
blocks.prompt: Points \(A\) and \(B\) represent \(a=-1 + 3 \mathrm{i}\) and \(b=2 - \mathrm{i}\). Give \(b-a\) as (real part, imaginary part) and the exact distance \(AB\).
blocks.hint: Length AB is the modulus after taking the difference.
blocks.solution:
Subtract start from finish: \(b-a=3 - 4 \mathrm{i}\).

The length is \(|b-a|=5\). Interchanging start and finish reverses the displacement and leaves its length unchanged.

sections.title: What happens to angle and length under conjugation?
sections.label: Reflect a direction
sections.intro: Conjugation keeps the horizontal coordinate and reverses the vertical coordinate. The distance from the origin is unchanged.

blocks.html: A non-zero number with argument \(\theta\) has a conjugate whose argument is \(-\theta\) modulo \(2\pi\). Put the result back into the specified interval.
At the negative real axis, taking the negative of the principal argument produces the excluded endpoint.

blocks.title: Choose the argument in the stated interval
blocks.prompt: Find the exact argument of \(- 2 \sqrt{3} - 2 \mathrm{i}\) in radians with \(-\pi<\theta\le\pi\).

retry.feedback: This direction points along the opposite ray. Use the signs of both coordinates.

blocks.hint: Sketch the signs of the Cartesian components before using an acute reference angle.
blocks.solution:
Use the point \(\left(- 2 \sqrt{3},-2\right)\) to fix the direction.

The signs put the point in quadrant III. The acute reference angle is \(\frac{\pi}{6}\). In the stated interval that gives \(- \frac{5 \pi}{6}\).

examples.title: Find distance from the origin
examples.question: Find the modulus of \(-7 + 24 \mathrm{i}\).
solution: The two Cartesian components are \(-7\) and \(24\).
By Pythagoras the modulus is \(\sqrt{(-7)^2+(24)^2}=25\).

examples.title: Choose the argument in the stated interval
examples.question: Find the exact argument of \(- 5 \sqrt{3} + 5 \mathrm{i}\) in radians with \(-\pi<\theta\le\pi\).
solution: Use the point \(\left(- 5 \sqrt{3},5\right)\) to fix the direction.
The signs put the point in quadrant II. The acute reference angle is \(\frac{\pi}{6}\). In the stated interval that gives \(\frac{5 \pi}{6}\).

examples.title: Choose the argument in the stated interval
examples.question: Find the exact argument of \(-4 - 4 \mathrm{i}\) in radians with \(-\pi<\theta\le\pi\).
solution: Use the point \(\left(-4,-4\right)\) to fix the direction.
The signs put the point in quadrant III. The acute reference angle is \(\frac{\pi}{4}\). In the stated interval that gives \(- \frac{3 \pi}{4}\).

examples.title: Choose the argument in the stated interval
examples.question: Find the exact argument of \(-9\) in radians with \(-\pi<\theta\le\pi\).
solution: Use the point \(\left(-9,0\right)\) to fix the direction.
The point lies on an axis. From the positive real axis, the required direction in the stated interval is \(\pi\).

examples.title: Recover Cartesian components from distance and direction
examples.question: A point has modulus \(6\) and argument \(- \frac{2 \pi}{3}\) radians. Give the (real part, imaginary part) pair.
solution: The horizontal component is \(r\cos\theta\); the vertical component is \(r\sin\theta\).
The two components are \(-3\) and \(- 3 \sqrt{3}\). Thus the number is \(-3 - 3 \sqrt{3} \mathrm{i}\).

examples.title: Use the Argand displacement between two points
examples.question: Points \(A\) and \(B\) represent \(a=2 - 3 \mathrm{i}\) and \(b=-3 + 9 \mathrm{i}\). Give \(b-a\) as (real part, imaginary part) and the exact distance \(AB\).
solution: Subtract start from finish: \(b-a=-5 + 12 \mathrm{i}\).
The length is \(|b-a|=13\). Interchanging start and finish reverses the displacement and leaves its length unchanged.

examples.title: Choose the argument in the stated interval
examples.question: Find the exact argument of \(- 3 \sqrt{2} - 3 \sqrt{2} \mathrm{i}\) in radians with \(0\le\theta<2\pi\).
solution: Use the point \(\left(- 3 \sqrt{2},- 3 \sqrt{2}\right)\) to fix the direction.
The signs put the point in quadrant III. The acute reference angle is \(\frac{\pi}{4}\). In the stated interval that gives \(\frac{5 \pi}{4}\).

orig_9709_p3_cx_polar.description: Choose a useful representation, multiply and divide with exact arguments, and find both square roots in polar or exponential form.

sections.title: When is polar or exponential form shorter?
sections.label: Choose a representation
sections.intro: Cartesian form gives signed coordinates. Polar form gives distance and angle, so multiplication and division become shorter.

blocks.html: \(e^{\mathrm i\theta}=\cos\theta+\mathrm i\sin\theta\). Therefore \(re^{\mathrm i\theta}\) and \(r(\cos\theta+\mathrm i\sin\theta)\) describe the same point.
Use radians in the exponential. The zero point does not have a direction angle.

blocks.title: Switch from Cartesian to polar form
blocks.prompt: Give the two parameters (modulus, argument in radians) of \(- 3 \sqrt{3} + 3 \mathrm{i}\) in polar form. Use \(-\pi<\theta\le\pi\).
blocks.hint: Find the radius and locate the quadrant before converting the angle.
blocks.solution:
Pythagoras gives the radius \(6\) from the components \(- 3 \sqrt{3}\) and \(3\).

The direction of the point from the origin gives angle \(\frac{5 \pi}{6}\) in the required interval.

In polar form this is \(6\left(\cos\left(\frac{5 \pi}{6}\right)+\mathrm i\sin\left(\frac{5 \pi}{6}\right)\right)\).

sections.title: Why do product angles add?
sections.label: Multiply in polar form
sections.intro: A product combines radii multiplicatively and turns successively. In exponential form the exponent rule already expresses these two steps.

blocks.html: \((re^{\mathrm i\alpha})(se^{\mathrm i\beta})=rse^{\mathrm i(\alpha+\beta)}\). Reduce the result to the interval requested.
Do not multiply the angles. A sum beyond the endpoint names the same ray after subtracting a whole turn.

blocks.title: Find the polar product
blocks.prompt: Take \(u=4e^{\mathrm i\left(\frac{5 \pi}{6}\right)}\) and \(v=3e^{\mathrm i\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)}\). Give \(uv\) as the pair (modulus, argument in radians), with \(-\pi<\theta\le\pi\).
blocks.hint: Use different operations for the moduli and angles. Add the angles and then use the stated interval.
blocks.solution:
Multiply the moduli to obtain \(12\).

Add the direction angles to obtain \(\frac{4 \pi}{3}\) before changing intervals.

Reduce by whole turns if needed. The requested angle is \(- \frac{2 \pi}{3}\), giving \(12e^{\mathrm i\left(- \frac{2 \pi}{3}\right)}\).

blocks.html: A product can finish in a different quadrant from either factor.

sections.title: Which angle comes first in a quotient?
sections.label: Divide in polar form
sections.intro: Use numerator direction minus denominator direction. The modulus of the divisor must be positive.

blocks.html: \(\frac{re^{\mathrm i\alpha}}{se^{\mathrm i\beta}}=\frac rs e^{\mathrm i(\alpha-\beta)}\), where \(s>0\).
Reversing the order of the angles reflects the quotient across the real axis.

blocks.title: Find the polar quotient
blocks.prompt: Take \(u=18e^{\mathrm i\left(- \frac{\pi}{6}\right)}\) and \(v=6e^{\mathrm i\left(\frac{2 \pi}{3}\right)}\). Give \(\frac uv\) as the pair (modulus, argument in radians), with \(0\le\theta<2\pi\).
blocks.hint: Use different operations for the moduli and angles. Subtract the angles and then use the stated interval.
blocks.solution:
Divide the moduli to obtain \(3\).

Subtract the direction angles to obtain \(- \frac{5 \pi}{6}\) before changing intervals.

Reduce by whole turns if needed. The requested angle is \(\frac{7 \pi}{6}\), giving \(3e^{\mathrm i\left(\frac{7 \pi}{6}\right)}\).

sections.title: What does multiplication do to the diagram?
sections.label: Scale and rotate
sections.intro: Multiplication by the same number changes the distance and angle of every point in the same way. Division uses the reciprocal change.

blocks.html: The rotation is about the origin. For a divisor of modulus r, the new distance is the old distance multiplied by its reciprocal.

figure.alt: A shorter ray in quadrant I and a longer image ray in quadrant II, showing an anticlockwise rotation about the origin and an increase in radius.
figure.caption: Multiplication by a fixed non-zero complex number scales the radius and rotates about the origin.

blocks.html: Adding a complex number translates the whole diagram. Multiplication keeps the origin fixed.

blocks.title: Identify the rotation and scale
blocks.prompt: The point for a non-zero \(z\) is sent to the point for \(\frac{z}{3e^{\mathrm i\left(- \frac{\pi}{6}\right)}}\). Select the radius multiplier and signed rotation in \((-\pi,\pi]\).
blocks.hint: Scale the distance from the origin, then rotate about the origin. Use the direction of the operation.
blocks.solution:
Dividing by a fixed complex number scales every radius by \(\frac{1}{3}\).

Subtract the argument of the fixed number. The corresponding rotation is \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) radians.

sections.title: Where does the second square root come from?
sections.label: Halve two full-turn alternatives
sections.intro: When a square is taken, many angles name the target. Use two target representatives a full turn apart before halving them.

blocks.html: For a non-zero target \(re^{\mathrm i\theta}\), take modulus \(\sqrt r\) and directions \(\frac{\theta}{2}\) and \(\frac{\theta}{2}+\pi\). Normalise each separately.
The two roots lie on opposite rays because the target’s full turn becomes a half-turn.

blocks.title: Find two square roots in exponential form
blocks.prompt: Find both square roots of \(36e^{\mathrm i\left(- \frac{\pi}{3}\right)}\). Enter both (modulus, argument in radians) pairs with \(-\pi<\theta\le\pi\).

retry.feedback: One root is correct. Add a half-turn and give the second root as a separate pair.

blocks.hint: Halve two angles for the original number which differ by a full turn.
blocks.solution:
Squaring doubles the direction and squares the modulus. Each root has modulus \(6\).

Doubling angles is modulo \(2\pi\), so first use \(- \frac{\pi}{3}\) and \(\frac{5 \pi}{3}\) as target directions.

Halve each angle and reduce to the stated interval. The two arguments are \(- \frac{\pi}{6}\) and \(\frac{5 \pi}{6}\).

The roots are opposite points on the Argand diagram.

blocks.html: Check both roots by doubling their angles and squaring their common modulus.

sections.title: When is the other square-root method better?
sections.label: Choose the final form
sections.intro: Use Cartesian comparison when the Cartesian parts are simple and the question needs exact Cartesian roots. Polar form makes the two directions visible.

blocks.html: On the negative real axis use the included argument pi if the principal interval is requested. Its two square-root rays are the positive and negative imaginary axes.
With a zero target, solve directly: its only distinct square root is zero.

blocks.title: Find two square roots in exponential form
blocks.prompt: Find both square roots of \(81\). Enter both (modulus, argument in radians) pairs with \(0\le\theta<2\pi\).

retry.feedback: One root is correct. Add a half-turn and give the second root as a separate pair.

blocks.hint: Halve two angles for the original number which differ by a full turn.
blocks.solution:
Squaring doubles the direction and squares the modulus. Each root has modulus \(9\).

Doubling angles is modulo \(2\pi\), so first use \(0\) and \(2 \pi\) as target directions.

Halve each angle and reduce to the stated interval. The two arguments are \(0\) and \(\pi\).

The roots are opposite points on the Argand diagram.

examples.question: Give the two parameters (modulus, argument in radians) of \(-5 + 5 \sqrt{3} \mathrm{i}\) in polar form. Use \(-\pi<\theta\le\pi\).
solution: Pythagoras gives the radius \(10\) from the components \(-5\) and \(5 \sqrt{3}\).

The direction of the point from the origin gives angle \(- \frac{\pi}{4}\) in the required interval.
In exponential form this is \(8e^{\mathrm i\left(- \frac{\pi}{4}\right)}\).

examples.title: Find the polar product
examples.question: Take \(u=2e^{\mathrm i\left(\frac{2 \pi}{3}\right)}\) and \(v=3e^{\mathrm i\left(\frac{3 \pi}{4}\right)}\). Give \(uv\) as the pair (modulus, argument in radians), with \(-\pi<\theta\le\pi\).
solution: Multiply the moduli to obtain \(6\).
Add the direction angles to obtain \(\frac{17 \pi}{12}\) before changing intervals.
Reduce by whole turns if needed. The requested angle is \(- \frac{7 \pi}{12}\), giving \(6e^{\mathrm i\left(- \frac{7 \pi}{12}\right)}\).

examples.title: Find the polar quotient
examples.question: Take \(u=12e^{\mathrm i\left(- \frac{2 \pi}{3}\right)}\) and \(v=4e^{\mathrm i\left(\frac{3 \pi}{4}\right)}\). Give \(\frac uv\) as the pair (modulus, argument in radians), with \(-\pi<\theta\le\pi\).
solution: Divide the moduli to obtain \(3\).
Subtract the direction angles to obtain \(- \frac{17 \pi}{12}\) before changing intervals.
Reduce by whole turns if needed. The requested angle is \(\frac{7 \pi}{12}\), giving \(3e^{\mathrm i\left(\frac{7 \pi}{12}\right)}\).

examples.title: Identify the rotation and scale
examples.question: The point for a non-zero \(z\) is sent to the point for \(2e^{\mathrm i\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)}z\). Select the radius multiplier and signed rotation in \((-\pi,\pi]\).
solution: Multiplying by a fixed complex number scales every radius by \(2\).
Add the argument of the fixed number. The corresponding rotation is \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) radians.

examples.title: Find two square roots in exponential form
examples.question: Find both square roots of \(25e^{\mathrm i\left(\frac{2 \pi}{3}\right)}\). Enter both (modulus, argument in radians) pairs with \(-\pi<\theta\le\pi\).
solution: Squaring doubles the direction and squares the modulus. Each root has modulus \(5\).
Doubling angles is modulo \(2\pi\), so first use \(\frac{2 \pi}{3}\) and \(\frac{8 \pi}{3}\) as target directions.
Halve each angle and reduce to the stated interval. The two arguments are \(\frac{\pi}{3}\) and \(- \frac{2 \pi}{3}\).
The roots are opposite points on the Argand diagram.

examples.title: Find two square roots in exponential form
examples.question: Find both square roots of \(49e^{\mathrm i\left(\pi\right)}\). Enter both (modulus, argument in radians) pairs with \(0\le\theta<2\pi\).
solution: Squaring doubles the direction and squares the modulus. Each root has modulus \(7\).
Doubling angles is modulo \(2\pi\), so first use \(\pi\) and \(3 \pi\) as target directions.
Halve each angle and reduce to the stated interval. The two arguments are \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\frac{3 \pi}{2}\).
The roots are opposite points on the Argand diagram.

orig_9709_p3_cx_loci.description: Turn modulus and argument conditions into circles, bisectors and rays, and identify shared regions with the correct boundaries.

sections.title: Why does a modulus condition give a circle?
sections.label: Distance from a fixed point
sections.intro: The value of a difference modulus is a distance from a fixed centre. Equal distance gives a boundary circle and an inequality chooses a side.

blocks.html: \(|z-a|=r\) is the circle centred at \(a\) with radius \(r>0\). The inequality \(|z-a|<r\) keeps the interior and \(|z-a|>r\) keeps the exterior.

figure.alt: A circle centred at the point a representing 1−2i. Its open interior is shaded and the circle boundary is drawn dashed.
figure.caption: The disk contains points less than the radius away from a. A dashed boundary is excluded.

blocks.html: Keep the sign of the centre. The expression z minus a means start the displacement at a.

blocks.title: Read a circle and its boundary
blocks.prompt: For \(|z-\left(3 - 4 \mathrm{i}\right)|\le5\), give the Cartesian equation of the circle centred at the fixed point. Then select the intended region.
blocks.hint: The inequality decides which side to shade and whether to draw the boundary solid or dashed.
blocks.solution:
The fixed point is \(3 - 4 \mathrm{i}\). Interpret the modulus as distance from \(\left(3,-4\right)\).

Setting the distance equal to \(5\) gives the boundary \(\left(x - 3\right)^{2} + \left(y + 4\right)^{2}=25\).

Inside the circle and on its boundary.

sections.title: Which points are equally far from two positions?
sections.label: Perpendicular bisectors
sections.intro: Take two fixed points. Points on their perpendicular bisector are the same distance from each of them.

blocks.html: \(|z-a|=|z-b|\) gives a line. Squaring both non-negative distances cancels the quadratic terms in the two variables.

figure.alt: Points A and B are separated by an oblique segment. A line through its midpoint is perpendicular to the segment.
figure.caption: Equal distances from A and B select their perpendicular bisector.

blocks.html: The locus goes through the midpoint and is perpendicular to the segment, rather than parallel to it.

blocks.title: Find the perpendicular bisector
blocks.prompt: Let \(a=-2 + 4 \mathrm{i}\) and \(b=4 + 2 \mathrm{i}\). Give the midpoint as (real part, imaginary part), then enter the Cartesian equation of \(|z-a|=|z-b|\).
blocks.hint: Set the squared distances equal and cancel the common squared variable terms.
blocks.solution:
The two moduli are non-negative distances. Equal distances define the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining the two fixed points.

The midpoint is \(1 + 3 \mathrm{i}\). After squaring the distances, the two squared variable terms cancel.

The resulting line is \(3 x - y=0\).

sections.title: Where does a shifted argument ray start?
sections.label: Shift the ray’s starting point
sections.intro: The displacement is \(z-a\). Put the endpoint at the point representing \(a\) and measure the direction from a horizontal ray pointing right.

blocks.html: \(\arg(z-a)=\alpha\) means \(z=a+t(\cos\alpha+\mathrm i\sin\alpha)\) for \(t>0\).
The opposite half of the same line has a different direction. The endpoint itself has no argument.

blocks.title: Identify a ray and its endpoint
blocks.prompt: For \(\arg\!\left(z-\left(1 + 4 \mathrm{i}\right)\right)=- \frac{\pi}{2}\), give the endpoint coordinates and choose the point that belongs to the locus.

retry.feedback: The zero displacement from the endpoint has no argument.

blocks.hint: Subtract the endpoint first. The correct point must be ahead of the endpoint in the given direction.
blocks.solution:
The argument measures the direction of the displacement from \(1 + 4 \mathrm{i}\), so the endpoint is \(\left(1,4\right)\).

Moving from the endpoint by \(- 3 \mathrm{i}\) follows the required ray and reaches \(1 + \mathrm{i}\).

The endpoint is excluded because the zero displacement has no argument.

sections.title: How do I shade points that satisfy two conditions?
sections.label: Keep their shared region
sections.intro: Sketch each boundary and mark which side meets its condition. A candidate point is in the shared region only if it meets both tests.

blocks.html: Use a solid boundary for equality allowed and dashed for equality excluded. When an argument is involved, mark an open circle at any excluded endpoint.

figure.alt: The shaded quarter-disc is above and to the right of its centre, excluding its lower ray and centre. The upper ray and quarter-circle arc are included where both restrictions hold.
figure.caption: Keep only the points that satisfy both tests.

blocks.html: A boundary included by one condition can still be excluded by the other.

blocks.title: Decide which point satisfies both restrictions
blocks.prompt: Let \(a=-1 + 3 \mathrm{i}\). Apply both restrictions \(|z-a|<4\) and \(0<\arg(z-a)\le\frac{\pi}{2}\). Which listed point is included?

retry.feedback: The angle is zero there. The lower limit is strict.
At the centre the argument is undefined.

blocks.hint: Check distance and direction separately. The horizontal boundary is excluded here.
blocks.solution:
Measure from \(-1 + 3 \mathrm{i}\). The circle limits how far the point can lie from the centre.

The angle limits select the quarter from just above the positive real direction up to and including the positive imaginary direction, measured from that centre.

The displacement to \(4 \mathrm{i}\) is \(1+\mathrm i\). It satisfies both restrictions. The centre has no direction.

sections.title: How do I calculate where boundaries meet?
sections.label: Find both intersections
sections.intro: Use coordinates when a circle boundary meets a line. \(\operatorname{Re}z=h\) is the vertical line \(x=h\). \(\operatorname{Im}z=k\) is the horizontal line \(y=k\).

blocks.html: Write \((x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2\) for centre \((h,k)\). A positive remaining square gives two intersection positions.
A valid intersection can lie on an excluded boundary of a region. State inclusion separately.

blocks.title: Find both intersections with a boundary
blocks.prompt: The circle \(|z-(-3 + 2 \mathrm{i})|=5\) meets the line \(y=5\). Enter both intersection coordinates as (x, y).

retry.feedback: This is one intersection. The second sign gives the other point.

blocks.hint: Substitute the fixed coordinate and take both signs of the remaining square root.
blocks.solution:
Write the circle as \(\left(x + 3\right)^{2} + \left(y - 2\right)^{2}=25\).

Substituting the fixed y-coordinate leaves a squared displacement of \(16\) in the other coordinate.

Taking both signs yields \(\left(-7,5\right),\quad \left(1,5\right)\).

sections.title: How can I check a boundary point at a glance?
sections.label: Test distance and direction
sections.intro: A candidate point can satisfy the correct distance condition and still fail the directional condition. Test the two quantities separately.

blocks.html: A point at the centre satisfies every positive-radius disc constraint. It fails a direction constraint based at that centre.
A non-strict upper angle bound does not make a strict lower angle bound inclusive.

blocks.title: Decide which point satisfies both restrictions
blocks.prompt: Let \(a=5 + 2 \mathrm{i}\). Apply both restrictions \(|z-a|\le3\) and \(0<\arg(z-a)\le\frac{\pi}{2}\). Which listed point is included?

retry.feedback: The angle is zero there. The lower limit is strict.
At the centre the argument is undefined.

blocks.hint: Check distance and direction separately. The horizontal boundary is excluded here.
blocks.solution:
Measure from \(5 + 2 \mathrm{i}\). The circle limits how far the point can lie from the centre.

The angle limits select the quarter from just above the positive real direction up to and including the positive imaginary direction, measured from that centre.

The displacement to \(6 + 3 \mathrm{i}\) is \(1+\mathrm i\). It satisfies both restrictions. The centre has no direction.

examples.title: Read a circle and its boundary
examples.question: For \(|z-\left(1 - 2 \mathrm{i}\right)|<3\), give the Cartesian equation of the circle centred at the fixed point. Then select the intended region.
solution: The fixed point is \(1 - 2 \mathrm{i}\). Interpret the modulus as distance from \(\left(1,-2\right)\).
Setting the distance equal to \(3\) gives the boundary \(\left(x - 1\right)^{2} + \left(y + 2\right)^{2}=9\).
Inside the circle, with the boundary excluded.

examples.title: Read a circle and its boundary
examples.question: For \(|z-\left(-2 + \mathrm{i}\right)|\le4\), give the Cartesian equation of the circle centred at the fixed point. Then select the intended region.
solution: The fixed point is \(-2 + \mathrm{i}\). Interpret the modulus as distance from \(\left(-2,1\right)\).
Setting the distance equal to \(4\) gives the boundary \(\left(x + 2\right)^{2} + \left(y - 1\right)^{2}=16\).
Inside the circle and on its boundary.

examples.title: Find the perpendicular bisector
examples.question: Let \(a=1 + 2 \mathrm{i}\) and \(b=5 + 4 \mathrm{i}\). Give the midpoint as (real part, imaginary part), then enter the Cartesian equation of \(|z-a|=|z-b|\).
solution: The two moduli are non-negative distances. Equal distances define the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining the two fixed points.
The midpoint is \(3 + 3 \mathrm{i}\). After squaring the distances, the two squared variable terms cancel.
The resulting line is \(2 x + y - 9=0\).

examples.title: Identify a ray and its endpoint
examples.question: For \(\arg\!\left(z-\left(2 - \mathrm{i}\right)\right)=\frac{\pi}{4}\), give the endpoint coordinates and choose the point that belongs to the locus.
solution: The argument measures the direction of the displacement from \(2 - \mathrm{i}\), so the endpoint is \(\left(2,-1\right)\).
Moving from the endpoint by \(1 + \mathrm{i}\) follows the required ray and reaches \(3\).
The endpoint is excluded because the zero displacement has no argument.

examples.title: Decide which point satisfies both restrictions
examples.question: Let \(a=2 + \mathrm{i}\). Apply both restrictions \(|z-a|\le3\) and \(0<\arg(z-a)\le\frac{\pi}{2}\). Which listed point is included?
solution: Measure from \(2 + \mathrm{i}\). The circle limits how far the point can lie from the centre.
The angle limits select the quarter from just above the positive real direction up to and including the positive imaginary direction, measured from that centre.
The displacement to \(3 + 2 \mathrm{i}\) is \(1+\mathrm i\). It satisfies both restrictions. The centre has no direction.

examples.title: Find both intersections with a boundary
examples.question: The circle \(|z-(2 - \mathrm{i})|=5\) meets the line \(x=6\). Enter both intersection coordinates as (x, y).
solution: Write the circle as \(\left(x - 2\right)^{2} + \left(y + 1\right)^{2}=25\).
Substituting the fixed x-coordinate leaves a squared displacement of \(9\) in the other coordinate.
Taking both signs yields \(\left(6,-4\right),\quad \left(6,2\right)\).

examples.title: Decide which point satisfies both restrictions
examples.question: Let \(a=3 - 2 \mathrm{i}\). Apply both restrictions \(|z-a|<5\) and \(0<\arg(z-a)\le\frac{\pi}{2}\). Which listed point is included?
solution: Measure from \(3 - 2 \mathrm{i}\). The circle limits how far the point can lie from the centre.
The angle limits select the quarter from just above the positive real direction up to and including the positive imaginary direction, measured from that centre.
The displacement to \(4 - \mathrm{i}\) is \(1+\mathrm i\). It satisfies both restrictions. The centre has no direction.

glossary.definition: A set of points that satisfies one condition.
The line of all points equidistant from two distinct points.
A half-line in a specified direction. For an argument condition the endpoint is excluded.
A boundary included by a non-strict distance condition.

Turn algebra into a picture

Read the fixed point before choosing a sketch.

ConditionLocus or region
\(|z-a|=r\)Circle with centre a and radius r.
\(|z-a|<r\)Interior only, with the circle excluded.
\(|z-a|=|z-b|\)Perpendicular bisector of the segment joining a and b.
\(\arg(z-a)=\alpha\)Ray from a, with a excluded.
revision.checks:
• Label axes and the fixed points.
  • For each inequality check which boundary points belong.
  • For simultaneous conditions shade only the overlap.
